steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our NLU paper on a cross-model comparative loss: the idea is that a full model should never do worse than versions of itself with some input or hidden neurons ablated, and we turn that into a training loss. Motivate it from pruning and context selection, explain the loss and how we build comparable ablated models, summarize the experiments, and list the contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Bigger models / longer context help on average, but not always: some neurons are dispensable or harmful
- Pruning and context selection remove bad neurons extrinsically; can we improve neuron utility intrinsically during training?
- Intuition: comparison principle between a full model and its ablated models
- Comparative loss: ranking loss over task-specific losses of full and ablated models
- Making ablated models comparable: progressive ablation, CmpDrop and CmpCrop
- Experiments and findings
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Bigger is not always better
  - NLU pushed forward by deep neural models
  - two conventional ways to improve: enlarge model size (cite) -> more hidden neurons; enlarge input context (cite) -> more input neurons
  - more neurons = higher accuracy on average, but large models don't always beat small ones
  - hidden side: pruning keeps accuracy with far fewer parameters (neuron connections) (cite), even improves generalization (cite); prior work: ablating neurons consistently improves some specific classes (cite); larger LMs worse on non-negligible fraction of instances (cite)
  - -> some hidden neurons dispensable or even obstructive
  - input side: QA (cite) and query understanding (cite): more context distracts the model, hurts performance
  - more input neurons = more relevant features but also more noise
- Extrinsic vs intrinsic
  - context selection methods (cite) trim noisy input segments by pre-processing, like pruning by post-processing
  - both reduce inefficient neurons via extra processing
  - question: can we intrinsically improve neuron utility during training?
- Comparison principle
  - ideal network: all neurons cooperate efficiently, max utility of each
  - ablate some input/hidden neurons (disable part of context or params) -> submodel should not do better, even if ablated neurons are noisy (efficient model already suppressed noise)
  - principle: fewer neurons ablated -> better performance
  - training: task-specific loss as proxy for performance, lower = better
  - Fig. 1 example: full model (a) minimal loss; if ablated (b) efficient in its restricted space, (d) loss > (b) since (d) ablates one more input neuron
- Comparative loss
  - gap between ideal model and reality (cite) -> enforce the principle during training
  - no additional manual supervision
  - ranking loss on top of multiple task-specific losses
  - losses from full model + several comparable ablated models, ablated to varying degrees
  - pairwise hinge loss: penalize fewer ablated neurons but larger loss; such pairs contribute loss difference; compliant pairs -> no loss
  - drives order of losses to match order of ablation degrees
  - theory: dynamic weighting of task-specific losses, adaptive weights by full/ablated model performance
- Comparability
  - prerequisite; Fig. 1 counterexample: (c) ablates fewer neurons than (d) but not comparable
  - progressive ablation: first ablated model = one ablation on full model; each later one = further ablation on previous -> comparable submodel
  - CmpDrop: ablate hidden neurons via dropout (cite), any dropout-compatible model
  - CmpCrop: ablate input neurons by cropping extraneous context segments, any task with extraneous input content
- Experiments
  - 14 datasets, 3 NLU tasks (text classification, QA, query understanding), prediction types classification / extraction / ranking
  - 5 widely used PLMs (cite)
  - beats state-of-the-art baselines; better utility of parameters and context
  - analysis: comparative loss weights task losses more appropriately, as derived
  - best: first CmpCrop then CmpDrop
  - especially effective for few-parameter or long-input models; lower-capacity models fit more/longer samples better; higher capacity inherently prone to fit less data -> less help
  - CmpDrop: task loss drops to lower levels faster; CmpCrop: alleviates overfitting somewhat
- Contributions
  - comparative loss, cross-model, based on comparison principle, no extra human supervision
  - progressive ablation + two controlled ablation methods (dropout, context cropping), wide range of tasks and models
  - theory of how it works + experiments on 3 NLU tasks; code and data at https://github.com/zycdev/CmpLoss

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Deep neural models have pushed natural language understanding (NLU) a big step forward. There are two conventional and effective ways to further improve the performance of deep models: make the model bigger and make the input context bigger. Making the model bigger adds more hidden neurons, and making the context bigger adds more input neurons. Models with more hidden or input neurons have higher accuracy on average, but large-scale models do not always beat small models. On the hidden side, many network pruning methods have shown that compressed models with far fewer parameters (neuron connections) can keep their accuracy and can even generalize better. Prior work also found that ablating neurons can consistently improve performance on some specific classes, and other work showed empirically that larger language models really do perform worse on a non-negligible fraction of instances. So some hidden neurons in the trained model are dispensable or even obstructive. On the input side, a lot of work on question answering and query understanding has noticed that feeding more context is more likely to distract the model and hurt performance. This is not surprising, because more input neurons mean more relevant features but also more noise that interferes with the model.

Many context selection methods trim noisy segments from the input context by pre-processing, which is similar to how network pruning cuts inefficient parameters by post-processing. Basically, both network pruning and context selection reduce inefficient hidden or input neurons by adding extra processing. But besides reducing inefficient neurons extrinsically like this, can we improve the utility of neurons intrinsically while the model is being trained?

Imagine an ideal neural network where all neurons cooperate efficiently so that the utility of each neuron is maximized. If we ablate some of the input or hidden neurons in this network (disabling part of the input context or the model parameters), the ablated submodel should not perform better, even if the ablated neurons are noisy. The reason is that an efficient model should have already suppressed this noise. From this intuition we get a rough comparison principle between the full model and its ablated model: the fewer neurons are ablated, the better the model should perform. During training we can use task-specific losses as a proxy for performance on training samples, where lower task-specific loss means better performance. For example, in Fig. 1 the task-specific loss of the efficient full model (a) should be minimal, and if the ablated model (b) is also efficient in its restricted parameter space, then the task-specific loss of the ablated model (d) should be greater than that of (b), since (d) ablates one more input neuron than (b).

- Comparative loss
  - gap between ideal model and reality (cite) -> enforce the principle during training
  - no additional manual supervision
  - ranking loss on top of multiple task-specific losses
  - losses from full model + several comparable ablated models, ablated to varying degrees
  - pairwise hinge loss: penalize fewer ablated neurons but larger loss; such pairs contribute loss difference; compliant pairs -> no loss
  - drives order of losses to match order of ablation degrees
  - theory: dynamic weighting of task-specific losses, adaptive weights by full/ablated model performance
- Comparability
  - prerequisite; Fig. 1 counterexample: (c) ablates fewer neurons than (d) but not comparable
  - progressive ablation: first ablated model = one ablation on full model; each later one = further ablation on previous -> comparable submodel
  - CmpDrop: ablate hidden neurons via dropout (cite), any dropout-compatible model
  - CmpCrop: ablate input neurons by cropping extraneous context segments, any task with extraneous input content
- Experiments
  - 14 datasets, 3 NLU tasks (text classification, QA, query understanding), prediction types classification / extraction / ranking
  - 5 widely used PLMs (cite)
  - beats state-of-the-art baselines; better utility of parameters and context
  - analysis: comparative loss weights task losses more appropriately, as derived
  - best: first CmpCrop then CmpDrop
  - especially effective for few-parameter or long-input models; lower-capacity models fit more/longer samples better; higher capacity inherently prone to fit less data -> less help
  - CmpDrop: task loss drops to lower levels faster; CmpCrop: alleviates overfitting somewhat
- Contributions
  - comparative loss, cross-model, based on comparison principle, no extra human supervision
  - progressive ablation + two controlled ablation methods (dropout, context cropping), wide range of tasks and models
  - theory of how it works + experiments on 3 NLU tasks; code and data at https://github.com/zycdev/CmpLoss

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Deep neural models have pushed natural language understanding (NLU) a big step forward. There are two conventional and effective ways to further improve the performance of deep models: make the model bigger and make the input context bigger. Making the model bigger adds more hidden neurons, and making the context bigger adds more input neurons. Models with more hidden or input neurons have higher accuracy on average, but large-scale models do not always beat small models. On the hidden side, many network pruning methods have shown that compressed models with far fewer parameters (neuron connections) can keep their accuracy and can even generalize better. Prior work also found that ablating neurons can consistently improve performance on some specific classes, and other work showed empirically that larger language models really do perform worse on a non-negligible fraction of instances. So some hidden neurons in the trained model are dispensable or even obstructive. On the input side, a lot of work on question answering and query understanding has noticed that feeding more context is more likely to distract the model and hurt performance. This is not surprising, because more input neurons mean more relevant features but also more noise that interferes with the model.

Many context selection methods trim noisy segments from the input context by pre-processing, which is similar to how network pruning cuts inefficient parameters by post-processing. Basically, both network pruning and context selection reduce inefficient hidden or input neurons by adding extra processing. But besides reducing inefficient neurons extrinsically like this, can we improve the utility of neurons intrinsically while the model is being trained?

Imagine an ideal neural network where all neurons cooperate efficiently so that the utility of each neuron is maximized. If we ablate some of the input or hidden neurons in this network (disabling part of the input context or the model parameters), the ablated submodel should not perform better, even if the ablated neurons are noisy. The reason is that an efficient model should have already suppressed this noise. From this intuition we get a rough comparison principle between the full model and its ablated model: the fewer neurons are ablated, the better the model should perform. During training we can use task-specific losses as a proxy for performance on training samples, where lower task-specific loss means better performance. For example, in Fig. 1 the task-specific loss of the efficient full model (a) should be minimal, and if the ablated model (b) is also efficient in its restricted parameter space, then the task-specific loss of the ablated model (d) should be greater than that of (b), since (d) ablates one more input neuron than (b).

Since there is a gap between the ideal model and reality, we want to enforce this necessity (the comparison principle) during training so that the model uses its neurons better. Based on this natural comparison principle between models, we propose a cross-model comparative loss that trains models without additional manual supervision. In general, the comparative loss is a ranking loss on top of multiple task-specific losses. The task-specific losses come from the full neural model and several comparable ablated models, whose neurons are ablated to different degrees. The ranking loss is a pairwise hinge loss that penalizes models with fewer ablated neurons but larger task-specific losses. More concretely, if a model with fewer ablated neurons gets a larger task-specific loss than another model with more ablated neurons, the difference between the two task-specific losses is added to the final comparative loss; if not, the pair follows the comparison principle and gives no training loss. This way the comparative loss pushes the order of the task-specific losses to match the order of the ablation degrees. We also show by theoretical derivation that comparative loss can be seen as a dynamic weighting of multiple task-specific losses, which assigns weights adaptively depending on how the full and ablated models perform.

Comparative loss needs the multiple ablated models to be comparable. This is a basic prerequisite. As a counterexample, the ablated model (c) in Fig. 1 ablates fewer neurons than (d), but they are not comparable, so no comparative loss can be applied to them. To make the ablated models comparable with each other, we ablate the models progressively. We get the first ablated model by doing one ablation on the full model. If we need more ablated models, at each next step we build a new ablated model by doing a further ablation on the ablated model from the previous step, so the new ablated model is certainly a comparable submodel of the previous ones. For each ablation step we provide two alternative controlled ablation methods, CmpDrop and CmpCrop. CmpDrop ablates hidden neurons using dropout, so in theory it works for all dropout-compatible models. CmpCrop ablates input neurons by cropping extraneous context segments, so in theory it works for all tasks that have extraneous content in the input context.

We apply comparative loss with CmpDrop and/or CmpCrop to 14 datasets from 3 NLU tasks (text classification, question answering and query understanding), which have different prediction types (classification, extraction and ranking), on top of 5 widely used pretrained language models (PLMs). The results show that comparative loss is effective compared to state-of-the-art baselines, and that the utility of parameters and context is improved. Our analysis also confirms that comparative losses really do weight multiple task-specific losses more appropriately, like our derivation says. When we try different comparison strategies, we see that comparing models ablated first by CmpCrop and then by CmpDrop gives the biggest improvement. Interestingly, comparative loss is especially effective for models with few parameters or long inputs. This may mean that comparative loss helps lower-capacity models fit more or longer training samples better, while higher-capacity models are inherently prone to fit less data, so comparative loss helps them less. We also find that the different ablation methods affect training differently: CmpDrop helps the task-specific loss go down to lower levels faster, and CmpCrop reduces overfitting to some extent.

Our main contributions are:

- We propose comparative loss, a cross-model loss function based on the comparison principle between the full model and its ablated models, which improves neuronal utility without additional human supervision.

- We ablate the models progressively so that multiple ablated models are comparable, and we present two controlled ablation methods based on dropout and context cropping that apply to a wide range of tasks and models.

- We show theoretically how comparative loss works and demonstrate its effectiveness empirically with experiments on 3 different natural language understanding tasks. The code and processed data are released at https://github.com/zycdev/CmpLoss.

steps.text:
Natural language understanding (NLU) has been pushed a remarkable step forward by deep neural models. Enlarging model size [1,2,3,4] and input context [5,6,7] are two conventional and effective ways to further enhance the performance of deep models, where the former introduces more hidden neurons and the latter brings more input neurons. Although neural models with more hidden or input neurons have higher accuracy on average, large-scale models do not always beat small models. On one hand, many network pruning methods have shown that compressed models with significantly reduced parameters (neuron connections) can maintain accuracy [8,9,10] and even improve generalization [11]; [12] find that ablation of neurons can consistently improve performance in some specific classes; and [13] empirically demonstrate that larger language models indeed perform worse on a non-negligible fraction of instances. These phenomena indicate that some hidden neurons in the currently trained model are dispensable or even obstructive. On the other hand, much of the work on question answering [14,15] and query understanding [16,17,18] has noted that feeding more contextual information is more likely to distract the model and hurt performance. This is not surprising, since more input neurons mean more relevant features but are also likely to introduce more noise that interferes with the model. Similar to network pruning, which cuts out inefficient parameters through post-processing, many context selection methods [19,20,21,22] trim off noisy segments from the input context by pre-processing. In essence, both reduce inefficient hidden or input neurons through additional processing. However, apart from extrinsically reducing inefficient neurons, can we intrinsically improve the utility of neurons during model training?

Imagine an ideal neural network in which all neurons cooperate efficiently to maximize the utility of each neuron. If a fraction of the input or hidden neurons in this network are ablated (disabling partial input context or model parameters), the ablated submodel should not perform better, even if the ablated neurons are noisy, because an efficient model should have already suppressed these noises. Following this intuition, we can roughly find a comparison principle between the original full model and its ablated model: the fewer neurons are ablated, the better the model should perform. During training, task-specific losses can serve as a proxy for model performance on training samples, with lower losses implying better performance. For example, the task-specific loss of the efficient full model (a) in Fig. 1 should be minimal, and if the ablated model (b) is also efficient with respect to its restricted parameter space, the task-specific loss of the ablated model (d) should be greater than that of (b) because (d) ablates one more input neuron than (b).

Noting the gap between the ideal model and reality [19,13], we aim to ensure this necessity (comparison principle) during training to improve the model's utilization of neurons. Based on the natural comparison principle between models, we propose a cross-model comparative loss to train models without additional manual supervision. In general, the comparative loss is a ranking loss on top of multiple task-specific losses. These task-specific losses are derived from the full neural model and several comparable ablated models whose neurons are ablated to varying degrees, and the ranking loss is a pairwise hinge loss that penalizes models that have fewer ablated neurons but larger task-specific losses. Concretely, if a model with fewer ablated neurons gets a larger task-specific loss than another model with more ablated neurons, the difference between the task-specific losses of the pair is taken into account in the final comparative loss; otherwise the pair complies with the comparison principle and incurs no training loss. In this way, the comparative loss drives the order of task-specific losses to be consistent with the order of the ablation degrees. Through theoretical derivation, we also show that comparative loss can be viewed as a dynamic weighting of multiple task-specific losses, adaptively assigning weights depending on the performance of the full/ablated models.

The comparability among multiple ablated models is a fundamental prerequisite for comparative loss. As a counterexample, although the ablated model (c) in Fig. 1 ablates fewer neurons than (d), the two are not comparable, so no comparative loss can be applied. To make the ablated models comparable with each other, we ablate the models progressively. The first ablated model is obtained by performing one ablation on the full model. If more ablated models are needed, each subsequent step constructs a new ablated model by performing a further ablation on top of the ablated model from the previous step, which makes the new model certainly a comparable submodel of the previous ones. We provide two alternative controlled ablation methods for each ablation step, called CmpDrop and CmpCrop. CmpDrop ablates hidden neurons by the dropout [23] technique and is theoretically applicable to all dropout-compatible models, while CmpCrop ablates input neurons by cropping extraneous context segments and is theoretically applicable to all tasks that contain extraneous content in the input context.

We apply comparative loss with CmpDrop or/and CmpCrop on 14 datasets from 3 NLU tasks (text classification, question answering and query understanding) with distinct prediction types (classification, extraction and ranking) on top of 5 widely used pretrained language models (PLMs) [24,25,26,27,28]. The empirical results demonstrate the effectiveness of comparative loss over state-of-the-art baselines, as well as the enhanced utility of parameters and context. Our analysis also confirms that comparative losses can indeed weight multiple task-specific losses more appropriately, as our derivation indicates. Exploring different comparison strategies, we observe that comparing the models ablated first by CmpCrop and then by CmpDrop brings the greatest improvement. Interestingly, comparative loss is particularly effective for models with few parameters or long inputs. This may imply that comparative loss helps models with lower capacity fit more or longer training samples better, while models with higher capacity are inherently prone to fit less data, so comparative loss is less helpful for them. Moreover, different ablation methods have different effects on training: CmpDrop helps the task-specific loss decrease to lower levels faster, and CmpCrop alleviates overfitting to some extent.

The main contributions can be summarized as follows:

- We propose comparative loss, a cross-model loss function based on the comparison principle between the full model and its ablated models, to improve neuronal utility without additional human supervision.

- We progressively ablate the models to make multiple ablated models comparable, and present two controlled ablation methods based on dropout and context cropping that are applicable to a wide range of tasks and models.

- We theoretically show how comparative loss works and empirically demonstrate its effectiveness through experiments on 3 distinct natural language understanding tasks. We release the code and processed data at https://github.com/zycdev/CmpLoss.
